claim: Tumors frequently exhibit aberrant glycosylation, which can impact cancer progression and therapeutic responses.
source: Tumors frequently exhibit aberrant glycosylation, which can impact cancer progression and therapeutic responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Akella et al., 2019; Mereiter et al., 2019; Munkley, 2019) as indicated in the Introduction section.

claim: The hexosamine biosynthesis pathway (HBP) produces uridine diphosphate N-acetylglucosamine (UDP-GlcNAc), a major substrate for glycosylation in the cell.
source: The hexosamine biosynthesis pathway (HBP) produces uridine diphosphate N-acetylglucosamine (UDP-GlcNAc), a major substrate for glycosylation in the cell.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the HBP pathway.

claim: Prior studies have identified the HBP as a promising therapeutic target in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA).
source: Prior studies have identified the HBP as a promising therapeutic target in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA).
evidence: This claim references prior research findings as discussed in the Introduction.

claim: The HBP requires both glucose and glutamine for its initiation.
source: The HBP requires both glucose and glutamine for its initiation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the HBP pathway requirements.

claim: Glutamine limitation in PDA cells suppresses de novo hexosamine synthesis.
source: Here, we identify that glutamine limitation in PDA cells suppresses de novo hexosamine synthesis but results in increased free GlcNAc abundance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically isotope tracing experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Glutamine limitation in PDA cells results in increased free GlcNAc abundance.
source: Here, we identify that glutamine limitation in PDA cells suppresses de novo hexosamine synthesis but results in increased free GlcNAc abundance.
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: GlcNAc salvage via N-acetylglucosamine kinase (NAGK) is engaged to feed UDP-GlcNAc pools.
source: GlcNAc salvage via N-acetylglucosamine kinase (NAGK) is engaged to feed UDP-GlcNAc pools.
evidence: This claim is supported by isotope tracing experiments with 13C-GlcNAc and NAGK knockout studies shown in Figure 3.

claim: NAGK expression is elevated in human PDA.
source: NAGK expression is elevated in human PDA, and NAGK deletion from PDA cells impairs tumor growth in mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data from human PDA tumors shown in Figure 4B.

claim: NAGK deletion from PDA cells impairs tumor growth in mice.
source: NAGK expression is elevated in human PDA, and NAGK deletion from PDA cells impairs tumor growth in mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo xenograft experiments shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation is upregulated in multiple cancers.
source: O-GlcNAcylation, the addition of a single N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) moiety onto a serine or threonine residue of intracellular proteins, is upregulated in multiple cancers (Akella et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Targeting O-GlcNAcylation suppresses the growth of breast, prostate, and colon cancer tumors.
source: Targeting O-GlcNAcylation suppresses the growth of breast, prostate, and colon cancer tumors (Caldwell et al., 2010; Ferrer et al., 2017; Gu et al., 2010; Guo et al., 2017; Lynch et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Highly branched N-glycan structures are sensitive to HBP flux and are upregulated in malignant tissue.
source: Similarly, highly branched N-glycan structures are sensitive to HBP flux and are upregulated in malignant tissue (Lau et al., 2007), and targeting the relevant Golgi GlcNAc transferase enzymes can limit tumor growth and metastasis in vivo (Granovsky et al., 2000; Li et al., 2008; Zhou et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Targeting Golgi GlcNAc transferase enzymes can limit tumor growth and metastasis in vivo.
source: Similarly, highly branched N-glycan structures are sensitive to HBP flux and are upregulated in malignant tissue (Lau et al., 2007), and targeting the relevant Golgi GlcNAc transferase enzymes can limit tumor growth and metastasis in vivo (Granovsky et al., 2000; Li et al., 2008; Zhou et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA) has a 5 year survival rate of 9%.
source: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA) is a deadly disease with a 5 year survival rate of 9% and a rising number of annual deaths (Rahib et al., 2014) (ACS Cancer Facts and Figures 2019, NIH SEER report 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to cancer statistics reports.

claim: Mutations in KRAS occur in nearly all cases of human PDA.
source: Mutations in KRAS occur in nearly all cases of human PDA and drive extensive metabolic reprogramming in cancer cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PDA genetics.

claim: Mutant KRAS drives extensive metabolic reprogramming in cancer cells.
source: Mutations in KRAS occur in nearly all cases of human PDA and drive extensive metabolic reprogramming in cancer cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about KRAS function in cancer.

claim: Enhanced flux into the HBP was identified as a primary metabolic feature mediated by mutant KRAS in PDA cells.
source: Enhanced flux into the HBP was identified as a primary metabolic feature mediated by mutant KRAS in PDA cells (Ying et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Hypoxia is a salient characteristic of the tumor microenvironment.
source: Hypoxia, a salient characteristic of the tumor microenvironment (Lyssiotis and Kimmelman, 2017), was shown to further promote expression of glycolysis and HBP genes in pancreatic cancer cells (Guillaumond et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Hypoxia promotes expression of glycolysis and HBP genes in pancreatic cancer cells.
source: Hypoxia, a salient characteristic of the tumor microenvironment (Lyssiotis and Kimmelman, 2017), was shown to further promote expression of glycolysis and HBP genes in pancreatic cancer cells (Guillaumond et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The glutamine analog 6-diazo-5-oxo-l-norleucine (DON) inhibits the HBP.
source: Notably, the glutamine analog 6-diazo-5-oxo-l-norleucine (DON), which inhibited the HBP, suppressed PDA metastasis, and sensitized PDA tumors to anti-PD1 therapy (Sharma et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: DON suppressed PDA metastasis.
source: Notably, the glutamine analog 6-diazo-5-oxo-l-norleucine (DON), which inhibited the HBP, suppressed PDA metastasis, and sensitized PDA tumors to anti-PD1 therapy (Sharma et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: DON sensitized PDA tumors to anti-PD1 therapy.
source: Notably, the glutamine analog 6-diazo-5-oxo-l-norleucine (DON), which inhibited the HBP, suppressed PDA metastasis, and sensitized PDA tumors to anti-PD1 therapy (Sharma et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: DON sensitizes PDA cells to the chemotherapeutic gemcitabine in vitro.
source: DON has also been reported to sensitize PDA cells to the chemotherapeutic gemcitabine in vitro (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: An inhibitor targeting the HBP enzyme phosphoacetylglucosamine mutase 3 (PGM3) enhances gemcitabine-mediated reduction of xenograft tumor growth in vivo.
source: Additionally, a recently developed inhibitor targeting the HBP enzyme phosphoacetylglucosamine mutase 3 (PGM3) enhances gemcitabine-mediated reduction of xenograft tumor growth in vivo (Ricciardiello et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The HBP has been proposed as a nutrient-sensing pathway since its rate-limiting step requires both glutamine and fructose-6-phosphate.
source: The HBP has been proposed as a nutrient-sensing pathway since its rate-limiting step, mediated by GFPT1/2, requires both glutamine and the glycolytic intermediate fructose-6-phosphate (Denzel and Antebi, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In hematopoietic cells, glucose deprivation limits UDP-GlcNAc levels and dramatically reduces levels of the N-glycoprotein IL3Rα at the plasma membrane in a manner dependent on the HBP.
source: In hematopoietic cells, glucose deprivation limits UDP-GlcNAc levels and dramatically reduces levels of the N-glycoprotein IL3Rα at the plasma membrane in a manner dependent on the HBP (Wellen et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation of certain nuclear-cytosolic proteins has been demonstrated to be nutrient sensitive, impacting protein stability or function.
source: Similarly, O-GlcNAcylation of certain nuclear-cytosolic proteins, including cancer-relevant proteins such as Myc and Snail, has been demonstrated to be nutrient sensitive, impacting protein stability or function (Housley et al., 2008; Park et al., 2010; Swamy et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The PDA tumor microenvironment is thought to be particularly nutrient poor, owing to its characteristic dense stroma.
source: Yet, the PDA tumor microenvironment is thought to be particularly nutrient poor, owing to its characteristic dense stroma (Halbrook and Lyssiotis, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: L-PHA binding was suppressed by glucose restriction in SW480 cells.
source: Indeed, L-PHA binding was suppressed by glucose restriction in SW480 cells and by glutamine restriction in both colon cancer cell lines (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: L-PHA binding was suppressed by glutamine restriction in both colon cancer cell lines.
source: Indeed, L-PHA binding was suppressed by glucose restriction in SW480 cells and by glutamine restriction in both colon cancer cell lines (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Across PDA cell lines, no consistent changes in L-PHA binding were observed under glucose or glutamine limitation.
source: Across these cell lines, no consistent changes in L-PHA binding were observed under glucose or glutamine limitation (Figure 1D,E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D, E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation was minimally altered by culture in low glutamine.
source: O-GlcNAcylation was minimally altered by culture in low glutamine and exhibited variable changes in response to glucose limitation (Figure 1F), consistent with stress-induced regulation of this modification (Taylor et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation exhibited variable changes in response to glucose limitation.
source: O-GlcNAcylation was minimally altered by culture in low glutamine and exhibited variable changes in response to glucose limitation (Figure 1F), consistent with stress-induced regulation of this modification (Taylor et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: TMG treatment resulted in equivalently elevated O-GlcNAcylation levels in high and low glutamine conditions.
source: TMG treatment resulted in equivalently elevated O-GlcNAcylation levels in high and low glutamine conditions (Figure 1G; Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), indicating that glutamine restriction does not limit the capacity of cells to add the O-GlcNAc modification.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Glutamine restriction does not limit the capacity of cells to add the O-GlcNAc modification.
source: TMG treatment resulted in equivalently elevated O-GlcNAcylation levels in high and low glutamine conditions (Figure 1G; Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), indicating that glutamine restriction does not limit the capacity of cells to add the O-GlcNAc modification.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the TMG treatment experiment shown in Figure 1G.

claim: In low glutamine conditions, GlcN-6-P levels were potently decreased relative to glutamine-replete conditions in PANC-1 cells.
source: In low glutamine conditions, GlcN-6-P levels were potently decreased relative to glutamine-replete conditions in PANC-1 cells, while UDP-GlcNAc abundance was maintained (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: UDP-GlcNAc abundance was maintained in low glutamine conditions in PANC-1 cells.
source: In low glutamine conditions, GlcN-6-P levels were potently decreased relative to glutamine-replete conditions in PANC-1 cells, while UDP-GlcNAc abundance was maintained (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In MIA PaCa-2 cells, UDP-GlcNAc abundance actually increased upon glutamine restriction.
source: In MIA PaCa-2 cells, UDP-GlcNAc abundance actually increased upon glutamine restriction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: UDP-GlcNAc abundance declined in 5 mM or 0.1 mM relative to 10 mM glucose conditions.
source: In contrast to that in glutamine restriction, UDP-GlcNAc abundance declined in 5 mM or 0.1 mM relative to 10 mM glucose conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that glutamine limitation specifically may trigger an adaptive response to sustain UDP-GlcNAc pools.
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Glutamine limitation specifically may trigger an adaptive response to sustain UDP-GlcNAc pools.
source: In contrast to that in glutamine restriction, UDP-GlcNAc abundance declined in 5 mM or 0.1 mM relative to 10 mM glucose conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that glutamine limitation specifically may trigger an adaptive response to sustain UDP-GlcNAc pools.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the metabolite data.

claim: Across multiple PDA cell lines, the fractional labeling of the glucosamine ring in both GlcNAc-P and UDP-GlcNAc pools was markedly suppressed by glutamine restriction.
source: Across multiple PDA cell lines, the fractional labeling of the glucosamine ring in both GlcNAc-P and UDP-GlcNAc pools was markedly suppressed by glutamine restriction, indicating decreased de novo synthesis in low glutamine conditions (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by 13C-glucose tracing experiments shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: Glutamine restriction indicates decreased de novo synthesis in low glutamine conditions.
source: Across multiple PDA cell lines, the fractional labeling of the glucosamine ring in both GlcNAc-P and UDP-GlcNAc pools was markedly suppressed by glutamine restriction, indicating decreased de novo synthesis in low glutamine conditions (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the isotope tracing data.

claim: Labeling into the ribose component of UDP-GlcNAc was suppressed by glutamine restriction.
source: Notably, labeling into the ribose component of UDP-GlcNAc was also suppressed (% labeled ribose indicates sum of isotopologs containing M+5 [i.e., M+5, M+7, M+11, and M+13]; Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by isotope tracing data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Incorporation of 13C glucose into UTP was suppressed upon glutamine restriction.
source: Consistently, incorporation of 13C glucose into UTP was suppressed upon glutamine restriction (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), even though UTP levels were maintained or increased (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), suggesting a role for nucleoside salvage in maintaining nucleotide pool in these conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by isotope tracing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: UTP levels were maintained or increased upon glutamine restriction.
source: Consistently, incorporation of 13C glucose into UTP was suppressed upon glutamine restriction (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), even though UTP levels were maintained or increased (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), suggesting a role for nucleoside salvage in maintaining nucleotide pool in these conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite measurements shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Nucleoside salvage plays a role in maintaining nucleotide pool in glutamine-deprived conditions.
source: Consistently, incorporation of 13C glucose into UTP was suppressed upon glutamine restriction (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), even though UTP levels were maintained or increased (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), suggesting a role for nucleoside salvage in maintaining nucleotide pool in these conditions.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the discrepancy between labeling and abundance.

claim: Autophagy/ribophagy is a source of nucleosides in amino acid-deprived conditions.
source: This is consistent with previous reports demonstrating that autophagy/ribophagy is a source of nucleosides in amino acid-deprived conditions (Guo et al., 2016a; Wyant et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Silencing of either of the uridine salvage enzymes uridine kinase 1 or 2 (UCK1/2) resulted in decreased UDP, UTP, and UDP-GlcNAc levels.
source: Indeed, silencing of either of the uridine salvage enzymes uridine kinase 1 or 2 (UCK1/2) resulted in decreased UDP, UTP, and UDP-GlcNAc levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C), indicating that nucleoside salvage contributes to maintaining uridine phosphate and UDP-GlcNAc pools.
evidence: This claim is supported by siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: Nucleoside salvage contributes to maintaining uridine phosphate and UDP-GlcNAc pools.
source: Indeed, silencing of either of the uridine salvage enzymes uridine kinase 1 or 2 (UCK1/2) resulted in decreased UDP, UTP, and UDP-GlcNAc levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C), indicating that nucleoside salvage contributes to maintaining uridine phosphate and UDP-GlcNAc pools.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the siRNA knockdown data.

claim: Glutamine restriction suppresses the de novo synthesis of both GlcNAc-P and UTP.
source: Thus, glutamine restriction suppresses the de novo synthesis of both GlcNAc-P and UTP, both of which are required to produce UDP-GlcNAc.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the isotope tracing data.

claim: Silencing of neither GALE nor GNE reduced UDP-GlcNAc labeling from glucose.
source: Silencing of neither GALE nor GNE reduced UDP-GlcNAc labeling from glucose, however, indicating that these enzymes are unlikely to facilitate a bypass pathway (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D,E.

claim: GALE and GNE are unlikely to facilitate a bypass pathway for UDP-GlcNAc synthesis.
source: Silencing of neither GALE nor GNE reduced UDP-GlcNAc labeling from glucose, however, indicating that these enzymes are unlikely to facilitate a bypass pathway (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the siRNA knockdown data.

claim: UDP-GlcNAc abundance is maintained despite reduced de novo hexosamine synthesis from glucose.
source: Regardless, the data clearly indicate that UDP-GlcNAc abundance is maintained despite reduced de novo hexosamine synthesis from glucose (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the metabolite and isotope tracing data.

claim: UDP-GlcNAc can be generated via phosphorylation of free GlcNAc by NAGK-generating GlcNAc-6-P.
source: As mentioned, UDP-GlcNAc can be generated via phosphorylation of free GlcNAc by NAGK-generating GlcNAc-6-P (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the GlcNAc salvage pathway.

claim: When supplemented, GlcNAc is salvaged into the UDP-GlcNAc pool.
source: When supplemented, GlcNAc is salvaged into the UDP-GlcNAc pool (Ryczko et al., 2016; Wellen et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Endogenous sources of GlcNAc may include removal of O-GlcNAc protein modifications or breakdown of glycoconjugates and extracellular matrix components.
source: Endogenous sources of GlcNAc may include removal of O-GlcNAc protein modifications or breakdown of glycoconjugates and extracellular matrix components.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential sources of GlcNAc.

claim: Intracellular levels of GlcNAc increase upon glutamine restriction.
source: Notably, intracellular levels of GlcNAc increase upon glutamine restriction (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: NAGK mRNA expression increased in PDA cell lines in low glutamine conditions.
source: NAGK mRNA expression increased in PDA cell lines in low glutamine conditions and in some cell lines also in low glucose (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: NAGK mRNA expression increased in some cell lines in low glucose.
source: NAGK mRNA expression increased in PDA cell lines in low glutamine conditions and in some cell lines also in low glucose (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: GFPT1 expression was induced in both low glucose conditions.
source: GFPT1 expression was also induced in both low glucose conditions, consistent with a prior report (Moloughney et al., 2016), and in low glutamine conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), even though de novo synthesis is suppressed when glutamine is limited.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: GFPT1 expression was induced in low glutamine conditions.
source: GFPT1 expression was also induced in both low glucose conditions, consistent with a prior report (Moloughney et al., 2016), and in low glutamine conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), even though de novo synthesis is suppressed when glutamine is limited.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Protein levels of NAGK did not increase in concordance with mRNA at these time points.
source: Protein levels of NAGK did not increase in concordance with mRNA at these time points, however, although a mobility shift potentially indicative of post-translational modification was apparent when protein lysates were run on a gel using a large electrophoresis system (see Materials and methods; Figure 2—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C,D.

claim: A mobility shift potentially indicative of post-translational modification was apparent for NAGK when protein lysates were run on a gel using a large electrophoresis system.
source: Protein levels of NAGK did not increase in concordance with mRNA at these time points, however, although a mobility shift potentially indicative of post-translational modification was apparent when protein lysates were run on a gel using a large electrophoresis system (see Materials and methods; Figure 2—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C,D.

claim: Removal of the phosphatase inhibitor Na3VO4 from the sample buffer prevented the mobility shift, suggesting that NAGK may be phosphorylated on one or more residues in low glutamine conditions.
source: Removal of the phosphatase inhibitor Na3VO4 from the sample buffer prevented the mobility shift, suggesting that NAGK may be phosphorylated on one or more residues in low glutamine conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D and is a speculative interpretation.

claim: Under low glutamine conditions, GlcNAc availability for salvage increases.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that under low glutamine conditions, GlcNAc availability for salvage increases and the salvage enzyme NAGK is subject to regulation.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the metabolite and gene expression data.

claim: The salvage enzyme NAGK is subject to regulation under low glutamine conditions.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that under low glutamine conditions, GlcNAc availability for salvage increases and the salvage enzyme NAGK is subject to regulation.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the gene expression and protein data.

claim: 13C GlcNAc was efficiently salvaged in control cells.
source: N-[1,2-13C2]acetyl-d-glucosamine (13C GlcNAc) was efficiently salvaged in control cells, and this was suppressed by NAGK deletion, as evidenced by reduced fractional labeling of GlcNAc-P and UDP-GlcNAc (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by isotope tracing data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 13C GlcNAc salvage was suppressed by NAGK deletion, as evidenced by reduced fractional labeling of GlcNAc-P and UDP-GlcNAc.
source: N-[1,2-13C2]acetyl-d-glucosamine (13C GlcNAc) was efficiently salvaged in control cells, and this was suppressed by NAGK deletion, as evidenced by reduced fractional labeling of GlcNAc-P and UDP-GlcNAc (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by isotope tracing data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Silencing of GALK2 further suppressed incorporation of 13C GlcNAc into GlcNAc-P and UDP-GlcNAc in the NAGK KO cells.
source: Indeed, silencing of GALK2 further suppressed incorporation of 13C GlcNAc into GlcNAc-P and UDP-GlcNAc in the NAGK KO cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In the absence of NAGK, increased glucose-dependent fractional labeling of the glucosamine ring of UDP-GlcNAc and GlcNAc-P was observed.
source: Indeed, in the absence of NAGK, we observed increased glucose-dependent fractional labeling of the glucosamine ring of UDP-GlcNAc and GlcNAc-P, but not the ribose component of UDP-GlcNAc (Figure 3C,D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by isotope tracing data shown in Figure 3C,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: In the absence of NAGK, the ribose component of UDP-GlcNAc was not increased in labeling from glucose.
source: Indeed, in the absence of NAGK, we observed increased glucose-dependent fractional labeling of the glucosamine ring of UDP-GlcNAc and GlcNAc-P, but not the ribose component of UDP-GlcNAc (Figure 3C,D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by isotope tracing data shown in Figure 3C,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: When NAGK is deleted and GlcNAc salvage is suppressed, de novo hexosamine synthesis increases.
source: Thus, when NAGK is deleted and GlcNAc salvage is suppressed, de novo hexosamine synthesis increases.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the isotope tracing data in NAGK knockout cells.

claim: In PANC-1 KO cells in 4 mM glutamine, GlcN-P increased significantly, consistent with increased de novo synthesis in the absence of NAGK.
source: In PANC-1 KO cells in 4 mM glutamine, GlcN-P increased significantly, consistent with increased de novo synthesis in the absence of NAGK (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite measurements shown in Figure 3E.

claim: GlcNAc-P was modestly reduced in PANC-1 NAGK KO cells.
source: GlcNAc-P was modestly reduced in KO cells, though UDP-GlcNAc levels were maintained (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite measurements shown in Figure 3E.

claim: UDP-GlcNAc levels were maintained in PANC-1 NAGK KO cells.
source: GlcNAc-P was modestly reduced in KO cells, though UDP-GlcNAc levels were maintained (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite measurements shown in Figure 3E.

claim: In MIA PaCa-2 cells, GlcNAc-P was markedly suppressed in the absence of NAGK.
source: In MIA PaCa-2 cells, GlcNAc-P was markedly suppressed in the absence of NAGK, though UDP-GlcNAc was not (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: UDP-GlcNAc was not markedly suppressed in MIA PaCa-2 NAGK KO cells.
source: In MIA PaCa-2 cells, GlcNAc-P was markedly suppressed in the absence of NAGK, though UDP-GlcNAc was not (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: GlcN-P decreased in control and KO cells under glutamine restriction, consistent with reduced de novo hexosamine synthesis.
source: GlcN-P decreased in control and KO cells, consistent with reduced de novo hexosamine synthesis (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite measurements shown in Figure 3E.

claim: GlcNAc-P levels decreased in low glutamine in control cells and decreased further in cells lacking NAGK.
source: GlcNAc-P levels decreased in low glutamine in control cells and decreased further in cells lacking NAGK, consistent with contributions from both de novo synthesis and salvage (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite measurements shown in Figure 3E.

claim: GlcNAc abundance was elevated upon glutamine limitation in both control and NAGK KO cells.
source: Reciprocally, GlcNAc abundance was elevated upon glutamine limitation in both control and NAGK KO cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite measurements shown in Figure 3E.

claim: UDP-GlcNAc abundance was modestly reduced in NAGK KO cells relative to controls under glutamine restriction.
source: UDP-GlcNAc abundance was modestly reduced in NAGK KO cells relative to controls under glutamine restriction, though levels were still comparable to that in high glutamine (Figure 3E), possibly reflecting changes in utilization.
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite measurements shown in Figure 3E.

claim: GALK2 silencing did not further suppress UDP-GlcNAc in NAGK KO cells.
source: GALK2 silencing did not further suppress UDP-GlcNAc in NAGK KO cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D), suggesting that GALK2 may not have a major role in physiological GlcNAc salvage.
evidence: This claim is supported by siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: GALK2 may not have a major role in physiological GlcNAc salvage.
source: GALK2 silencing did not further suppress UDP-GlcNAc in NAGK KO cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D), suggesting that GALK2 may not have a major role in physiological GlcNAc salvage.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the siRNA knockdown data.

claim: GlcNAc is salvaged into UDP-GlcNAc pools in PDA cells in a manner dependent at least in part on NAGK.
source: Cumulatively, the data demonstrate that GlcNAc is salvaged into UDP-GlcNAc pools in PDA cells in a manner dependent at least in part on NAGK.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the isotope tracing and metabolite data.

claim: Minimal differences in growth were found between NAGK KO cells and controls in 2D and 3D culture in 4 mM glutamine.
source: To test the role of NAGK in cell proliferation, we first monitored growth of NAGK KO cells compared to controls in 2D and 3D culture in 4 mM glutamine, finding minimal differences (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: MIA PaCa-2 KO cells died more quickly in 0.05 mM glutamine than did control cells.
source: Indeed, MIA PaCa-2 KO cells died more quickly in 0.05 mM glutamine than did control cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: PANC-1 KO cells did not show increased death in 0.05 mM glutamine.
source: PANC-1 KO cells did not show this effect (Figure 4A), but we hypothesized that NAGK loss might have a stronger effect in vivo where tumor growth can be constrained by nutrient availability.
evidence: This claim is supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: GFPT1 expression was increased in tumor tissue.

claim: Final tumor volume and weight were markedly reduced in the absence of NAGK.

evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo xenograft tumor measurements shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: Initial tumor growth was comparable between control and KO cells, but the NAGK knockout tumors either stopped growing or shrank while control tumors continued to grow larger.
